newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rates ease in more positive S.Africa money market.
newsitem.headline: Rates ease in more positive S.Africa money market.

text.p: South African money market rates fell slightly on Wednesday as positive sentiment crept back into the market, traders said.
"Generally there's a bit of positive sentiment coming in...we can hardly talk about pressure easing but there's a hint of better conditions," a trader commented.

Three-month negotiable certificate of deposit (NCD) rates have fallen to 17.35 percent offered from 17.40 percent, while the 90-day BA rate was between 16.65 and 16.95 percent against 16.70 to 17.00 percent earlier in the week.
The Reserve Bank said the money market shortage -- below 10 billion rand but still exerting some pressure on commercial banks -- was 9.686 billion rand on Tuesday from 9.499 billion on Monday.
Traders said there had been good demand for NCD rates and sentiment at the short end of the yield curve was very positive.

"Call rates have come down from around 18.00/18.25 percent to 17.50/17.75 so pressure is down on the very short end of the curve where most of the guys fund their books on a daily overnight basis," one said.
But others noted there were no signs of underlying change in economic fundamentals, and said the improved conditions were a seasonal phenomenon.
"The shortage traditionally tends to come down in the first week in January because everyone has finished spending in December and money flows back into the banks," one commented.
"It's a hint of things to come but the trigger has not necessarily been pulled," the trader said.
Another said the next two weeks would be decisive in gauging whether the trend would be positive. "It's too soon to tell and at this point in time...none of the fundamentals have changed," he said.

There had been positive signs in December in the money supply and private sector credit extension situation but it would take a couple of months to assess the direction of major economic indicators such as the balance of payments, he added.
